chapter.name: System of Elections
chapter.blurb: Constitutional basis of elections, the RPA 1950 and 1951, disputes and funding, party recognition criteria, delimitation and the ECI versus State Election Commissions.

scope_in.item: Articles on elections, voting system and stages of the election process, RPA 1950 and 1951
Election disputes, reform committees, political funding, symbols, proposers and criteria for national and state parties
Delimitation, other election Acts, Rules and Orders, ECI versus SEC and memory points

scope_out.item: Section 10 of RPA 1951 as undischarged insolvency, Law Commission 2018 report and the named list of national parties
scope_out.reason: conflicts with settled law or the standard textbook, or time-bound

skipped.reason: verify-conflict: Section 10 RPA 1951 deals with disqualification for contracts/offices with Government, not insolvency (that is Articles 102 and 191)

verify-conflict: recommendations of the doubtful 2018 report

concepts.name: Constitutional framework, voting system, election stages and the Representation of the People Acts
concepts.description: Articles 324-327, universal adult suffrage, FPTP, the stages from schedule to constitution of the House, the RPA 1950 and 1951 and the registration and recognition of parties.
concepts.idea: Elections rest on Articles 324-327, are run in set stages under first-past-the-post, and the RPA 1950 (rolls, seats) and RPA 1951 (conduct, disqualification, parties) fill the legal framework.
concepts.rule: Article 324 vests control of elections in the ECI; Article 243K and 243ZA create State Election Commissions for Panchayats and Municipalities; Article 325 bars exclusion from rolls on religion, race, caste or sex; Article 326 gives adult suffrage (age 18). India uses single-member constituencies, one roll per constituency and first past the post on EVMs with VVPAT. The stages run from the announcement of the schedule (which brings the Model Code into force) through notification, nominations, scrutiny, withdrawal, oath, campaign, polling, counting and results to constitution of the House. The RPA 1950 covered rolls, voter qualifications and seat allocation; the RPA 1951, enacted under Article 327, covers conduct, disqualifications (Section 8, Section 10A), registration of parties (Section 29A), offences, disputes and by-elections. Recognised parties are classified after elections and get symbols, free materials and media access.
concepts.example: A proposal for a separate roll for one community contravenes Article 325; a candidate with 28 per cent of valid votes in a five-way contest still wins.

questions.q: A State proposes to prepare a separate electoral roll for voters of one religious community in a constituency, apart from the general roll. Which constitutional provision does this most directly contravene?
questions.a: Article 325, which bars special rolls and exclusion on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex
o: Article 325, which bars special rolls and exclusion on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex
Article 324, which makes the Election Commission responsible for preparing separate rolls for each community
Article 326, which fixes 21 years as the minimum age for registration on any roll
Article 327, which allows Parliament to create special rolls for backward communities
questions.e: Article 325 says no person is ineligible for inclusion in the electoral roll, or may claim inclusion in a special roll, on grounds only of religion, race, caste or sex. The Constitution thus provides one general roll per territorial constituency.
w: Article 324 vests superintendence, direction and control of elections in the ECI; it says nothing of community rolls.
Article 326 provides for adult suffrage; the voting age is 18 (61st Amendment), and it is not the provision on special rolls.
Article 327 only empowers Parliament to legislate on elections; it creates no community roll.

questions.q: The Constitution provides for State Election Commissions to conduct elections to local bodies. Which of the following correctly pairs the Article with the local body it covers?
questions.a: Article 243K for Panchayats and Article 243ZA for Municipalities
o: Article 243K for Panchayats and Article 243ZA for Municipalities
Article 243ZA for Panchayats and Article 243K for Municipalities
Article 243D for Panchayats and Article 243T for Municipalities
Article 243E for Panchayats and Article 243U for Municipalities
questions.e: Article 243K (Panchayats) and Article 243ZA (Municipalities), inserted by the 73rd and 74th Amendments, create the State Election Commission; Articles 243D/243T (reservation) and 243E/243U (duration) are different provisions.
w: The two Articles are swapped: 243K is Panchayats and 243ZA is Municipalities.
243D and 243T deal with reservation of seats in Panchayats and Municipalities, not with the State Election Commission.
243E and 243U deal with the duration of Panchayats and Municipalities, not with the State Election Commission.

questions.q: Voting in a Lok Sabha election takes place on Electronic Voting Machines attached to VVPAT units. Which one of the following is the constitutional basis of the franchise exercised at that polling?
questions.a: Article 326, the adult-suffrage provision for Lok Sabha and Assembly polls
o: Article 326, the adult-suffrage provision for Lok Sabha and Assembly polls
Article 325, the adult-suffrage provision for Lok Sabha and Assembly polls
Article 324, which lays down the adult franchise that the Election Commission must enforce
Article 327, which grants adult suffrage to every citizen of India
questions.e: Polling by EVMs with VVPAT is conducted on the basis of adult suffrage under Article 326. Articles 324, 325 and 327 cover the Commission, non-discrimination in rolls and Parliament's law-making power respectively.
w: Article 325 bars exclusion from rolls on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex; adult suffrage is Article 326.
Article 324 vests superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Commission; it does not define the franchise.
Article 327 is Parliament's power to make laws on elections, not the grant of the franchise.

questions.q: Which one of the following is the event after which the Model Code of Conduct for parties and candidates comes into force in an election?
questions.a: The announcement of the election schedule by the Election Commission
o: The announcement of the election schedule by the Election Commission
The issue of the notification calling upon the electorate to elect members of the House, after the schedule is announced
The filing of the first nomination paper by a candidate in any constituency
The completion of scrutiny of nominations by the Returning Officer
questions.e: Once the ECI announces the election schedule, the Model Code of Conduct comes into effect immediately; the notification follows, and only then do nominations begin.
w: The notification comes after the schedule is announced and the Code is already in force by then.
Candidates file nominations only after the notification; the Code applies from the schedule announcement.
Scrutiny follows nominations; it is a later stage than the one that triggers the Code.
tr: Trigger of the Code vs start of formal process

questions.q: The Representation of the People Act, 1950 did not complete the legal framework of elections. Which one of the following matters was left to be provided by the later Act of 1951?
o: Allocation of seats in the House of the People and the Legislative Assemblies
Preparation of electoral rolls for constituencies
Qualifications of voters for registration in the rolls
questions.e: The 1950 Act dealt with rolls, voter qualifications and the allocation of seats/delimitation. Conduct of elections, offences, corrupt practices, disqualification of candidates, disputes and by-elections were left to the 1951 Act.
w: Allocation of seats was already provided by the 1950 Act.
Preparing the rolls was a subject of the 1950 Act.
Voter qualifications were dealt with by the 1950 Act.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the features of elections in India:

1. Article 326 makes adult suffrage the basis of voting for the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies, while Article 327 empowers Parliament to legislate on elections.
2. Lok Sabha and State Assembly elections are held in single-member territorial constituencies.
3. The Lok Sabha is elected by proportional representation through the single transferable vote.
4. Votes are cast on Electronic Voting Machines.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: Article 326 is the adult-suffrage provision. Statement 2 is correct: Each constituency elects one representative. Statement 3 is incorrect: India follows the First Past the Post system, not proportional representation, for the Lok Sabha. Statement 4 is correct: EVMs are used for polling. Also.
w: '2, 3 and 4 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 1, which is correct:
'1 and 2 only' leaves out statement 4, which is correct:
'2 and 4 only' leaves out statement 1, which is correct:

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about disqualification from voting in India:

1. A person may be disqualified from voting on the ground of being an undischarged insolvent.
2. A person may be disqualified from voting on the ground of non-residence.
3. A person of unsound mind may be disqualified from voting.
4. A person guilty of corrupt or illegal practices may be disqualified from voting.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: the grounds are non-residence, unsound mind, crime and corrupt or illegal practices; insolvency is not one of them. Statement 2 is correct: non-residence is a ground. Statement 3 is correct: unsoundness of mind is a ground. Statement 4 is correct: corrupt or illegal practices are a ground. Also
w: '1, 2 and 4 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 3, which is correct:
'2 and 3 only' leaves out statement 4, which is correct:
'3 and 4 only' leaves out statement 2, which is correct:

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the stages of an election:

1. Candidates may withdraw their candidature before their nominations are scrutinised, but not afterwards.
2. The oath or affirmation by candidates is taken only after the results are declared.
3. Candidates file nominations within the prescribed time after the notification, which specifies the nomination and polling dates.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: Withdrawal is allowed after scrutiny; validly nominated candidates may withdraw within two days of scrutiny. Statement 2 is incorrect: The oath/affirmation is a candidate's stage before campaigning. Statement 3 is correct: The notification starts the process and gives the dates; nominations follow. Also
w: '1 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 3, which is correct:
'2 only' includes statement 2, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 3, which is correct:
'2 and 3 only' includes statement 2, which is incorrect:

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the election process in India:

1. The election campaign is regulated by the Model Code of Conduct.
2. Polling is conducted through EVMs along with VVPAT.
3. After results are declared, the elected representatives assume office and the new House is constituted.
4. Counting of votes is conducted under the supervision of the State Election Commission.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: The Code regulates the campaign. Statement 2 is correct: Polling is conducted through EVMs with VVPAT. Statement 3 is correct: This is the last stage. Statement 4 is incorrect: Counting is conducted under the supervision of the Election Commission of India; the State Election Commission handles local-body polls. Also
w: '1, 3 and 4 only' includes statement 4, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 2, which is correct:
'1 and 3 only' leaves out statement 2, which is correct:
'2, 3 and 4 only' includes statement 4, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 1, which is correct:

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Representation of the People Act, 1951:

1. Article 324 is the constitutional source under which Parliament enacted the 1951 Act.
2. It forms the substantive law of elections in India.
3. Its qualification and disqualification provisions complement Articles 84, 102, 173 and 191.
4. One of its objectives is to regulate the conduct of elections.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: Parliament enacted it under Article 327; Article 324 vests control of elections in the Election Commission. Statement 2 is correct: It is the substantive law. Statement 3 is correct: These Articles are complemented by the Act. Statement 4 is correct: Conduct of elections is a stated objective. Also
w: '1, 3 and 4 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 2, which is correct:
'1, 2, 3 and 4' includes statement 1, which is incorrect:
'3 and 4 only' leaves out statement 2, which is correct:

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about provisions of the Representation of the People Act, 1951:

1. Section 8 provides for disqualification on conviction for certain criminal offences.
2. Section 10A provides for disqualification for failure to lodge the account of election expenses.
3. Section 29A provides for the registration of political parties with the Election Commission.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: Section 8 is the conviction provision. Statement 2 is correct: That is Section 10A. Statement 3 is correct: Registration of parties is under Section 29A. Also(registration of political parties).
w: '1 and 2 only' leaves out statement 3, which is correct:
'2 and 3 only' leaves out statement 1, which is correct:
'1 and 3 only' leaves out statement 2, which is correct:

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the privileges linked to recognition of political parties:

1. Candidates of recognised parties receive a fixed contribution towards their election expenses from public funds.
2. Candidates of recognised parties receive a free supply of specified election materials.
3. Candidates of recognised parties are allotted common election symbols.
4. Candidates of recognised parties get access to public media during campaigns, regulated separately.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: no such State funding exists; the privileges are in kind, such as materials, symbols and media access. Statement 2 is correct: this is one of the privileges. Statement 3 is correct: recognised parties receive their symbols. Statement 4 is correct: regulated access to public media is a privilege. Hence the answer is 2, 3 and 4 only.
w: '1, 2 and 3 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 4, which is correct
'2 and 3 only' leaves out statement 4, which is correct
'1, 2, 3 and 4' includes statement 1, which is incorrect

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the objectives of the Representation of the People Act, 1951:

1. Corrupt practices and electoral offences are defined by orders of the Election Commission and not by the Act itself.
2. It prescribes the qualifications and disqualifications of elected representatives.
3. It governs the registration and recognition of political parties and provides a legal mechanism for resolving election disputes.
4. By-elections and the filling of vacancies are outside the scope of the Act.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: defining and penalising corrupt practices and electoral offences is an objective of the Act itself. Statement 2 is correct: a stated objective. Statement 3 is correct: registration and recognition of parties and a mechanism for election disputes are stated objectives. Statement 4 is incorrect: regulating by-elections and the filling of vacancies is one of its objectives. Hence the answer is 2 and 3 only.
w: '3 and 4 only' includes statement 4, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 2, which is correct
'1, 2 and 3 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect
'2 and 4 only' includes statement 4, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 3, which is correct

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

1. An election is the formal process by which citizens choose their representatives or leaders by voting.
2. The Election Commission derives its powers of superintendence, direction and control over elections from Article 324.
3. Every citizen aged 21 years or above has the right to vote under the principle of universal adult suffrage.
4. Each stage of the election process is legally regulated to prevent malpractice and ensure fairness.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: this is the definition of an election. Statement 2 is correct: Article 324 vests superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Election Commission. Statement 3 is incorrect: the voting age is 18, lowered from 21 by the 61st Amendment. Statement 4 is correct: every stage of the electoral process is regulated by the Constitution, the Representation of the People Acts of 1950 and 1951 and the Commission's orders. So '1, 2 and 4 only' is correct.
w: '2, 3 and 4 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 1, which is correct:
'1 and 4 only' leaves out statement 2, which is correct:
'1, 2, 3 and 4' includes statement 3, which is incorrect:

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the election process:

1. The election notification officially starts the electoral process and specifies dates such as those of nomination and polling.
2. After nominations are scrutinised, validly nominated candidates may withdraw voluntarily.
3. Counting of votes is conducted under the supervision of the Election Commission of India.
4. The oath or affirmation by candidates is a stage that follows the declaration of results.

How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: True. Statement 2 is correct: True. Statement 3 is correct: True. Statement 4 is incorrect: It is a candidate stage before the campaign and polling. So 3 statement(s) are correct. Also
w: 'Only one' is not the right count: exactly 3 of the statements are correct.
'Only two' is not the right count: exactly 3 of the statements are correct.
'All four' is not the right count: exactly 3 of the statements are correct.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the recognition of political parties:

1. After elections, the ECI classifies registered parties as national parties, state parties and registered-but-unrecognised parties.
2. The recognition system serves orderly party competition, regulation of symbols and privileges, and transparency in functioning.
3. A party's recognition depends on its registration under the Act and not on its electoral performance.

How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: True. Statement 2 is correct: True. Statement 3 is incorrect: Recognition depends on electoral performance, not merely on registration. So 2 statement(s) are correct. Also
w: 'Only one' is not the right count: exactly 2 of the statements are correct.
'Only three' is not the right count: exactly 2 of the statements are correct.
'None of the statements' is not the right count: exactly 2 of the statements are correct.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Representation of the People Acts of 1950 and 1951:

1. The 1950 Act dealt with electoral rolls, voter qualifications and the allocation of seats.
2. The 1950 Act regulated by-elections to fill vacancies.
3. The 1951 Act deals with the delimitation of constituencies.
4. The 1951 Act fixes the qualifications of voters for inclusion in the rolls.

How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: True. Statement 2 is incorrect: By-elections are regulated by the 1951 Act. Statement 3 is incorrect: Delimitation and allocation of seats relate to the 1950 Act and the Delimitation Acts. Statement 4 is incorrect: Voter qualifications belong to the 1950 Act. So 1 statement(s) are correct. Also
w: 'Only two' is not the right count: exactly 1 of the statements are correct.
'Only three' is not the right count: exactly 1 of the statements are correct.
'None of the statements' is not the right count: exactly 1 of the statements are correct.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

Statement-I: In a Lok Sabha constituency, a candidate can be declared elected while polling less than half of the valid votes.
Statement-II: India follows the First Past the Post system, under which the candidate securing the highest number of votes in a single-member constituency wins.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
questions.a: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Statement-I is correct: the highest vote-getter wins even without an absolute majority. Statement-II is correct and explains it, since plurality in a single-member constituency requires no majority.
w: Rejected: II is the rule that makes I possible.
Rejected: II is correct, so the pair is not half-correct.
Rejected: I is correct; absolute majority is not needed.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

Statement-I: Candidates of recognised political parties receive a free supply of specified election materials.
Statement-II: Recognition as a national or state party follows automatically from registration, without regard to a party's electoral performance.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
questions.a: Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
o: Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Statement-I is correct: (a privilege of recognised parties). Statement-II is incorrect: recognition depends on electoral performance, not merely on registration.
w: Rejected: Statement-II is wrong, so the pair cannot both be correct.
Rejected: no explanation holds, since II is false.
Rejected: I is correct and II is the wrong one.

questions.q:
Pair each Article or Section in List-I with its subject in List-II.

List-I
A. Article 325
B. Article 327
C. Section 10A of the RPA 1951
D. Section 29A of the RPA 1951

List-II
1. Registration of political parties with the Election Commission
2. Disqualification for failure to lodge election expense accounts
3. Parliament's power to make laws on elections
4. Equality in roll inclusion: religion, race, caste or sex cannot bar a person
questions.e: A-4: Article 325 bars exclusion from rolls on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex. B-3: Parliament enacted the 1951 Act under Article 327. C-2: Section 10A is failure to lodge expense accounts. D-1: Section 29A is registration of parties.
w: Articles 325 and 327 are interchanged.
Sections 10A and 29A are interchanged.
A and C are interchanged; Article 325 is the non-exclusion article.

concepts.name: Corrupt practices, election disputes, funding reforms, symbols and criteria for national and state parties
concepts.description: Offences and election petitions, the Goswami and Gupta Committees, corporate cap and Electoral Bonds (struck down 2024), symbols, proposers, star campaigners, NOTA, VVPAT, deposits and criteria for recognition.
concepts.idea: Election disputes go only to the High Court with appeal to the Supreme Court, and recognition as a national or state party depends on set vote and seat thresholds.
concepts.rule: Bribery, undue influence, appeals on religion, race, caste or community, false statements and booth capturing are corrupt practices or offences; civil courts are barred and election petitions lie to the High Court with appeal to the Supreme Court. The Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) and the Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998) dealt with money power and State funding; the 7.5 per cent corporate cap was lifted in 2017 and the Electoral Bond Scheme (2018) was struck down by the Supreme Court in February 2024. A recognised party candidate needs one proposer and others ten; star campaigner limits are 40 and 20. A national party needs 6 per cent in four states plus 4 seats, or 2 per cent of the Lok Sabha seats (11) from three states, or state-party status in four states; a state party needs one of five conditions (6 per cent plus 2 seats, 6 per cent plus 1 Lok Sabha seat, 3 per cent of seats or 3 seats, 1 seat per 25, or 8 per cent of votes). Further reforms include NOTA (2013), VVPAT and the 2009 security deposits.
concepts.example: A voter who alleges a corrupt practice must file an election petition before the High Court; a civil suit is barred.

questions.q: A voter alleges that the winner of a Lok Sabha constituency won by a corrupt practice. Which of the following is the correct way to challenge the result?
questions.a: By an election petition before the High Court, tried on natural-justice lines in time-bound proceedings
o: By an election petition before the High Court, tried on natural-justice lines in time-bound proceedings
By a civil suit before the principal civil court of the district, since election results are ordinary civil disputes
By a petition filed in the first instance before the Supreme Court, which tries all election disputes
By a complaint to the Election Commission, which can set the result aside after hearing the parties
questions.e: The RPA 1951 bars civil courts in election matters; results can be challenged only by election petition before the High Court, tried under natural justice with time-bound proceedings. The scheme preserves finality while giving judicial oversight.
w: Civil court jurisdiction in election matters is barred.
Election petitions are filed before the High Court; the Supreme Court hears appeals.
The Commission cannot set aside a result; election petitions go to the High Court.

questions.q: Among the functions of the Election Commission, what role does it play when a question arises about the disqualification of a legislator?
questions.a: It advises the President in the case of an MP and the Governor in the case of a member of a State legislature
o: It advises the President in the case of an MP and the Governor in the case of a member of a State legislature
It advises the Governor in the case of an MP and the President in the case of a member of a State legislature
It advises the Speaker or Chairman of the House concerned in the case of both MPs and State legislators
It plays no part, as disqualification matters are left to the courts without any reference to it
questions.e: Under Article 103(2) the President decides a question of disqualification of a Member of Parliament in accordance with the opinion of the Election Commission, and under Article 192(2) the Governor does so for a member of a State legislature. This is an advisory role in disqualification matters.
w: The authorities are swapped.
The advice goes to the President/Governor, not to the presiding officers.
The Commission has an advisory function in disqualification matters.

questions.q: Under the nomination rules for a Lok Sabha or an Assembly constituency, how many electors must propose a candidate set up by a recognised party and a candidate who is an independent?
questions.a: One for the recognised-party candidate and ten for the independent
o: One for the recognised-party candidate and ten for the independent
Ten for the recognised-party candidate and ten for the independent
One for the recognised-party candidate and fifty for the independent
Five for the recognised-party candidate and ten for the independent
questions.e: A recognised party's candidate needs one proposer; candidates of unrecognised parties and independents need ten registered electors of the constituency.
w: Only the candidate not sponsored by a recognised party needs ten proposers.
Fifty is the number for a Presidential nomination, not this.
A recognised-party candidate needs one proposer.

questions.q: Parties may name star campaigners whose travelling expenditure is not counted in the candidate's account. Which pair correctly gives the limit for recognised parties and for registered-unrecognised parties?
questions.a: Up to 40 for recognised parties and up to 20 for registered-unrecognised parties
o: Up to 40 for recognised parties and up to 20 for registered-unrecognised parties
Up to 20 for recognised parties and up to 40 for registered-unrecognised parties
Up to 40 for recognised parties and up to 10 for registered-unrecognised parties
Up to 30 for both categories of parties
questions.e: As commonly stated, recognised parties may name 40 star campaigners and registered-unrecognised parties 20. Separately, Section 77 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 exempts the travelling expenditure of campaigning leaders from the candidate's election expenses.
w: The numbers are interchanged.
Registered-unrecognised parties may name 20, not 10.
The two categories have different limits: 40 and 20.

questions.q: A committee on electoral reforms was constituted in 1990 with special attention to money power in elections, and suggested partial State contribution to election funding along with transparent private donations. Which one is it?
questions.e: The Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990, set up under the National Front Government) focused on money power and recommended partial State contribution, transparent donations and stronger disclosure.
w: It was constituted in 1998 and dealt with State funding.
It examined the nexus between crime and politics in 1993.
It was an unofficial committee of 1974 appointed by Jayaprakash Narayan.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Dinesh Goswami and Indrajit Gupta Committees:

1. The Dinesh Goswami Committee recommended that private donations to parties should be transparent and accountable.
2. The Dinesh Goswami Committee recommended stronger disclosure norms to curb black money in elections.
3. The 1998 committee under Indrajit Gupta looked at whether State funding of elections was feasible.
4. The Indrajit Gupta Committee recommended partial State funding, particularly for recognised national and State parties.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: a recommendation of the committee. Statement 2 is correct: a recommendation of the committee. Statement 3 is correct: that was its remit. Statement 4 is correct: it favoured partial, not complete, funding. Hence the answer is 1, 2, 3 and 4.
w: '1, 2 and 3 only' leaves out statement 4, which is correct
'1, 3 and 4 only' leaves out statement 2, which is correct
'1, 2 and 4 only' leaves out statement 3, which is correct

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about political funding reforms:

1. In 2024 the Supreme Court upheld the Electoral Bond Scheme as a valid instrument of clean political funding.
2. The Electoral Bond Scheme, announced in the 2017 budget, was brought into force through a 2018 notification.
3. The 2017 budget lifted the 7.5 per cent of net profit cap on corporate contributions to political parties.
4. A citizen or an Indian entity could buy an electoral bond, which carried no buyer's name.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: in February 2024 the Supreme Court struck the scheme down as unconstitutional (ADR v Union of India). Statement 2 is correct: the scheme was announced in 2017 and notified in 2018. Statement 3 is correct: the Finance Act, 2017 removed the cap of 7.5 per cent of net profit. Statement 4 is correct: as described in the scheme.
w: '1, 3 and 4 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 2, which is correct.
'3 and 4 only' leaves out statement 2, which is correct.
'1, 2 and 3 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 4, which is correct.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about committees on electoral reforms:

1. The committee on State funding of elections headed by Indrajit Gupta was constituted in 1990.
2. The Dinesh Goswami Committee was constituted in 1990.
3. The Tarkunde Committee of 1974 was set up unofficially during the movement led by Jayaprakash Narayan, not by the Government.
4. The Vohra Committee, which reported in 1993, was concerned with State funding of elections.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: the Indrajit Gupta committee was constituted in 1998. Statement 2 is correct: the Dinesh Goswami Committee was appointed in 1990. Statement 3 is correct: the Tarkunde Committee (1974) was a non-governmental committee formed during the Jayaprakash Narayan movement. Statement 4 is incorrect: the Vohra Committee's subject was the nexus between crime and politics. Hence the answer is 2 and 3 only.
w: '1 and 3 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 2, which is correct
'1, 2 and 3 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect
'3 only' leaves out statement 2, which is correct

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the classification of political parties and their symbols:

1. The Election Commission recognises parties as national or state parties on electoral performance, and a national party's reserved symbol is valid throughout India.
2. A state party's reserved symbol is valid throughout India so long as the party contests in more than one state.
3. Registered-unrecognised parties choose their symbols from a list of free symbols.
4. Symbols help voters identify candidates, especially where illiteracy is high.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: parties are recognised as national or state parties on electoral performance, and a national party's reserved symbol is valid throughout India under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order. Statement 2 is incorrect: a state party's reserved symbol is valid only in the state(s) in which it is recognised. questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the conditions for recognition as a national party:

1. A party winning 2 per cent of the Lok Sabha seats qualifies if those seats come from any two states.
2. State-party status in four or more states is itself a ground for recognition as a national party.
3. A party securing 6 per cent of valid votes in four or more states, together with four Lok Sabha seats from any state(s), qualifies.
4. The list of national parties is fixed once and is not revised after general elections.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: the seats (at least 11) must come from at least three different states. Statement 2 is correct: one of the three conditions. Statement 3 is correct: one of the three conditions. Statement 4 is incorrect: the list is dynamic and revised after each general election. Hence the answer is 2 and 3 only.

Match each item in List-I with the corresponding figure in List-II on party recognition.

List-I
A. Minimum Lok Sabha seats under the 2 per cent condition for a national party
B. Share of total valid votes in the state, in either Lok Sabha or Assembly election, for a state party

questions.e: A-3: at least 11 Lok Sabha seats. B-2: 8 per cent of valid votes. C-1: four states. D-4: one seat for every 25 allotted.

concepts.name: Delimitation, election Acts and Rules, ECI versus State Election Commission and the Model Code
concepts.description: Delimitation Acts and Commissions, the 42nd, 84th and 87th Amendments, finality of orders, election Acts, Rules and Orders, appointment of election commissioners and the legal status of the Model Code of Conduct.
concepts.idea: Delimitation redraws boundaries on the 2001 Census while total seats stay on the 1971 basis, and the ECI and State Election Commissions have separate spheres.
concepts.rule: Articles 82 and 170 provide for readjustment after every Census and Articles 330 and 332 for SC and ST seats. Delimitation Acts were passed in 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002; the 42nd Amendment froze seats at the 1971 Census level, the 84th (2001) extended the freeze to the first Census after 2026 and the 87th (2003) based delimitation on the 2001 Census. Boundaries and SC/ST seats were redrawn on the 2001 Census without changing the total number of seats. Orders of the statutory Delimitation Commission are final and cannot be modified by the House. Several Acts, Rules and Orders (1950s-1992) support elections. The ECI conducts elections to Parliament, State Legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President; the State Election Commission conducts local body polls. The voting age was reduced to 18 by the 61st Amendment (1988). The Model Code of Conduct has no direct statutory backing.
concepts.example: A Gram Panchayat election is scheduled by the State Election Commission, not by the ECI.

questions.q: A political party challenges in the High Court a final order of the Delimitation Commission redrawing the boundaries of a Lok Sabha constituency. Which of the following describes the legal position?
questions.a: The order has the force of law, cannot be questioned in any court, and the House cannot modify it
o: The order has the force of law, cannot be questioned in any court, and the House cannot modify it
The order is open to challenge by writ in the High Court, as the Commission is a statutory and not a constitutional body
The order takes effect only after the Lok Sabha approves it, and the House may modify it by a simple majority
The order is binding only on the Election Commission, and Parliament may reject it by an ordinary law at any time
questions.e: Delimitation Commission orders are final: they cannot be challenged in any court and, when laid before the Lok Sabha or the State Assembly, cannot be modified. The Constitution also bars courts from questioning laws on delimitation or allotment of seats.
w: Its orders are final and cannot be challenged in any court.
The orders are laid before the House but modifications are not permissible.
The orders have the force of law and cannot be rejected by the Houses on being laid.

questions.q: A State Government wants the schedule of a Gram Panchayat election in its State to be fixed by the Election Commission of India under Article 324. Which of the following is the correct position?
questions.a: The State Election Commission, under Article 243K, a State-level body independent of the ECI
o: The State Election Commission, under Article 243K, a State-level body independent of the ECI
The ECI may fix it, since Article 324 covers all elections held in the country, local bodies included
The Delimitation Commission fixes it, since it controls all constituency-level electoral arrangements
The Governor fixes it directly, since Article 243ZA vests the schedule in the Governor
questions.e: Panchayat elections come under the State Election Commission (Article 243K); municipalities under Article 243ZA. The ECI conducts elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, President and Vice-President, and does not conduct local body elections.
w: Article 324 covers elections to Parliament, State Legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President, not local bodies.
The Delimitation Commission demarcates constituencies; it does not schedule elections.
Article 243ZA is the State Election Commission for Municipalities, and neither Article gives the schedule to the Governor.

questions.q: Which one of the following lowered the minimum age for voting from 21 years to 18 years?
questions.e: The 61st Amendment (1988) lowered the voting age from 21 to 18.
w: The 42nd Amendment froze seats at the 1971 Census level; it did not change the voting age.
The 62nd extended the reservation of seats for SC and ST in legislatures.
The 73rd gave constitutional status to Panchayats.

questions.q: Which one of the following correctly describes the legal status of the Model Code of Conduct?
questions.a: It has no direct statutory backing; the ECI enforces it through Article 324 and limited RPA 1951 provisions
o: It has no direct statutory backing; the ECI enforces it through Article 324 and limited RPA 1951 provisions
It is a schedule to the Representation of the People Act, 1951, and any breach disqualifies the candidate for six years
It is a part of the Constitution under Article 329, enforceable by the High Court
It is a statutory order of Parliament made under Article 327 and tried by Election Tribunals
questions.e: The Code has no direct statutory backing. It evolved by consensus among the political parties, who agreed to it in 1968, and the Commission first used it effectively in 1991.
w: The Code is not part of the Act and a breach does not automatically disqualify.
It is not a constitutional provision.
It is not a statutory order; it evolved by consensus among parties.

Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Statement-I is correct: under Article 103(2) the Commission advises the President on the disqualification of Members of Parliament. Statement-II is correct: under Article 192(2) it advises the Governor on members of State legislatures. The two are parallel functions for different legislatures; the second does not give a reason for the first.
w: Statement-II is a parallel function and not a reason for Statement-I.
Both authorities are correctly named, so Statement-II is correct.
Statement-I is correct: the President is advised on MPs.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

Statement-I: In elections held after 1 May 2015, ballot papers and EVMs carry the candidate's photograph with name and party symbol.
Statement-II: The Election Commission noted that candidates with the same or similar names often contest from one constituency, confusing voters.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
questions.a: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Statement-I is correct: the Commission's order applies to elections after 1 May 2015. Statement-II is correct: the Commission cited the confusion caused by namesake candidates as the reason for the order, so II explains I.
w: Statement-II is the stated reason for the photograph order, so it does explain Statement-I.
Statement-II is correct: namesake candidates are the problem noted.
Statement-I is correct: the order covers elections after 1 May 2015.

questions.q:
Match each Rules or Order in List-I with the matter it covers in List-II.

List-I
A. Registration of Electors Rules, 1960
B. The 1961 Rules for the Conduct of Elections
C. Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968
D. Registration of Political Parties (Furnishing of Additional Particulars) Order, 1992

List-II
1. Smooth, free and fair polls for Parliament and the State Legislatures
2. Specification, reservation and allotment of symbols, and recognition of parties
3. Additional particulars required for registering a party with the ECI
4. Preparing and publishing the electoral rolls
questions.e: A-4: 1960 Rules govern rolls. B-1: 1961 Rules facilitate free and fair conduct of elections. C-2: the 1968 Order deals with symbols and recognition. D-3: the 1992 Order prescribes particulars for registering a party.
w: A and B are interchanged: the 1960 Rules are about rolls.
C and D are interchanged: the 1968 Order is about symbols.
A and C are interchanged: rolls versus symbols.
